newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Italy tells Milosevic, Serbian opposition to talk.
newsitem.headline: Italy tells Milosevic, Serbian opposition to talk.

text.p: Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini on Thursday urged the Serbian opposition to back away from demands that President Slobodan Milosevic accept its victory at last month's local elections.

"Reinstatement of results (of the November 17 poll) seems to me to be something that is not on the cards as the basis for dialogue between the parties. They must find a formula around the impasse," he told a news conference.
Dini met Milosevic and then three leaders of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition to find ways of opening dialogue between the two rival groups.
"I think the conversations were constructive and I did not find any intention to stall the current situation and continue the impasse," he said.

The talks took place as students and opposition supporters jammed the city streets in another demonstration marking the 25th day of protests of alleged electoral fraud which overturned the results of local elections on November 17.
But in contrast to United States and European Parliament statements insisting Milosevic respect democracy, Dini argued that the opposition must back away from its basic demand to reach common ground.

Political analysts said the Italian minister's remarks would confirm opposition suspicions that the West is not serious about undermining Milosevic's grip on power for fear of destabilising the fragile Balkan peace.

Dini warned that both sides were still a long way from resolving their dispute over the elections which Zajedno says were stolen from it when local electoral authorities overturned opposition victories citing "irregularities".
"We found both the government and the opposition have dug themselves firmly into the positions from which they started," he said.

After meeting Dini, one of the three opposition leaders, Vuk Draskovic underlined Zajedno's position, insisting that there was "no possibility" of dialogue until the results of the November 17 elections were recognised.

"Absolutely not. The first condition is that Mr Milosevic must respect the electoral will of the people and recognise the results of November 17. After that we are ready for dialogue," Draskovic said.
Dini said he came on his own initiative to learn more about the dispute, and not as a representative of the EU, where he is a member of the "troika" of past, present and future presidents.
He also insisted Italy had no plans to act as mediator in the dispute which has brought up to 150,000 protesters onto the streets of Belgrade in daily demonstrations.
The United States earlier cancelled a meeting between Milosevic and its chief Balkans negotiator John Kornblum as part of its isolation of the Serbian president.
Italy said it notified the United States and NATO of Dini's Belgrade visit, but it was not immediately clear if the two organisations backed the initiative.
